about: Ahus (Áhús, modern Åhus in Skåne): one port, written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/ahus.md. A draft in the game's own files, for the user to overwrite. Every person here is invented: no one of this place is named in any source before 1149. Woven into the region danes_norway on 7 Oct 2026 by the region's weaver: ties made to run both ways, people named in ties made real in their own ports or pointed at the right id, stories given beats and cards in the other ports, and the region's cards (encounters/danes_norway_793.json) named in the sites' 'do' lists.

ports.summary: In 793 this is a town of craftsmen on the north bank of the Holy River, a short way up from the sea: about a hundred fenced plots on sand, and on nearly every one somebody cuts combs, casts brooches, works amber, forges knives or spins thread finer than you have seen. No king's man meets you and no coin is taken at its face: silver is weighed, nicked and cut. A merchant comes for whole sets of fine dress, combs, locked chests and knives, and brings antler, raw amber, scrap bronze, silver and beads.
ports.seasons: The town is fullest in winter: many craftsmen go away with the ships from the first day of summer to the winter nights and work the markets of the coast, and come home to their own hearths when the boats are drawn up. Herring comes to the bay in autumn and is cheap by the winter nights; ice lies along the shore after Yule (a guess), and the river runs brown into the bay all year.

history.text: About this year a market begins on the south bank of the river, a few hundred paces upstream: used for short spells, with shelters only. Beads are made there on a great scale, with bronze casting, comb-making and smithing. With Ribe it is the earliest such place in the north.
history.source: J. Callmer, 'North-European trading centres and the Early Medieval craftsman', Uppåkrastudier 6 (Lund 2002), 125-157 (Åhus I)

history.text: About this year the town on the north bank begins, in a strip of plots along the river. Within a generation it doubles inland. The bead-makers stop: beads from the west and from the Saracens' lands come in by the thousand, unstrung, cheaper than they can be made.

The town is at or near its full size: over twelve hectares, about a hundred plots of about 25 by 20 metres, five hundred to a thousand people, several hundred of them craftsmen who work for the whole coast.

Anskar, sailing for Birka, is robbed by pirates at sea of nearly forty books and the emperor's gifts. Where the books went is not recorded; the game lets what is left of them come ashore here or on Gotland.
history.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 10 (Robinson 1921); the sale here is the game's guess (?)

history.text: In the second half of this century the town is given up, probably moved a short way; the ground is ploughed from then on. Brooches of a ninth-century kind were still being cast here before the end.
history.source: Callmer 2002; where it moved to is not known (Elleköpinge is the usual guess (?))

history.text: About 880 to 890 Wulfstan sails from Haddeby to Truso with Skåne on his left hand: 'Langland, Laaland, Falster and Sconey, on his left, and all these lands belong to Denmark.'
history.source: Old English Orosius, tr. J. Bosworth (1859): texts_793.json 'wulfstan'

history.text: About the middle of this century Skåne comes firmly under the Danish king, Harald Gorm's son.
About this year King Sven founds Lund, two days' ride to the south-west. The first churches in Skåne are of these years.

'This year went King Knute to Denmark with a fleet to the holm by the holy river; where against him came Ulf and Eglaf, with a very large force both by land and sea, from Sweden. There were very many men lost on the side of King Knute, both of Danish and English; and the Swedes had possession of the field of battle.' Other accounts put it in 1026, name Olaf of Norway and Anund of the Svear as his enemies, and say Knute won. Whether it was this river or one in Uppland is disputed.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1025, tr. J. Ingram (1823), https://avalon.law.yale.edu/medieval/ang11.asp ; Wikipedia (en, sv) 'Battle of Helgeå'

history.text: About the middle of this century a house of stone is built by the river mouth, about twenty metres by ten: perhaps the oldest stone castle in the north. Who built it is not known.
Lund is made a bishop's seat.

eras.text: The craft town at its fullest. Rows of fenced plots along the river with open lanes between, a low workshop hut dug into the sand on each, smoke from casters' and smiths' hearths, boats drawn up on the bank and traders sleeping aboard them. No king's officer, no toll that anyone can name, no coin taken by count. In winter every hearth is lit; in summer a third of the men are away at other markets.

The town thins. Some plots stand empty and their fences are burnt; the casters still pour brooches of the new fashion, and dirhams are common enough to be cut without comment. Families talk of moving. A stranger notices that the lanes are wider than the traffic needs.

The town is gone and ploughed over. What is left is a landing at the river mouth among farms: herring in autumn, cattle, a boat or two for hire, a ship on the Baltic road putting in for water and news. Skåne answers to the Danish king when there is one strong enough to ask. What the place sells is the game's guess (?): no market is known here in these years.

The king's Skåne. Lund is founded and priests come through; some farms have a cross on the wall and a hammer under the shirt. King's coin is known but is still weighed. In 1025 or 1026 the bay is full of fleets for a summer and no cargo passes.

A house of stone stands by the river mouth, the first anyone here has seen, and whoever sits in it takes a share of what is landed. Herring boats crowd the beach in autumn. The old town is a field where the plough turns up bits of antler and green bronze.

sites.name: The bank under the town
sites.see: A brown river a hundred paces wide between low sandy banks, and open country with hardly a tree. In front, a dozen clinker boats drawn up or lying to a stone, some with a tent rigged over the hold and a cooking fire beside them: traders live aboard. Behind, fences and thatch in long rows, thin smoke, and the tap of hammers. It smells of tar, wet sand and burning oak.
sites.source: Callmer 2002: traders 'may have stayed on board their ships anchored or beached on the riverbank below the site'; the river from Research/water_levels/baltic_east.md

sites.name: The open place
sites.see: A bare trodden square in the middle of the plots, fifty paces by thirty, with lanes running out of it wide enough for two carts. Goods lie on hides and chest lids: combs in rows, brooches in pairs, knives, strings of beads, bundles of antler, a farmer's amber in a sack. Women string beads as they talk. Every dealer has a small folding scale, and nobody shouts a price.
sites.source: Callmer 2002: one open space of at least 50 by 30 m; lanes of 10 to 20 m; beads bought unstrung by the thousand. The scales are the spine's (silver_road); no weights are reported from the dig I read (?)

sites.name: Toke's plot
sites.see: A fenced plot on the oldest strip, right above the bank. A small house on the ground, and beside it a hut sunk knee-deep in the sand with its roof at shoulder height: inside, a bench by the door for the light, a heap of sawn antler, a row of comb plates waiting for their teeth, clay moulds drying. A dog gnaws something under the bench. It smells of scorched horn.
sites.source: Callmer 2002: sunken-floored huts as workshops and stores; one plot cast brooches, cut combs and worked amber; 28,136 pieces of antler waste

sites.name: The fire plots
sites.see: Three plots downwind where the hearths are: a smith's with a stone anvil and a heap of cauldron sheet waiting for rivets, and two casters' with crucibles no bigger than an egg cup glowing in charcoal. Broken clay moulds crunch underfoot. A man weighs scrap bronze against a row of lead weights; another files a key. Only men work at the fires.
sites.source: Callmer 2002: 3,596 mould pieces, 532 crucible pieces, about 100 kg of slag, chest locks, keys, riveted cauldron sheet; that fire crafts were forbidden to women he calls likely, not proven (?)

sites.name: The spinning huts
sites.see: A sunken hut with the door-flap tied back and four women in the light of it. Spindles turn with whorls no bigger than a hazelnut; an upright loom leans on the back wall with its weights swinging. One woman weaves a patterned ribbon on a little antler comb held in her lap. Outside, a sail lies over the fence with a bone needle stuck in the seam.
sites.source: Callmer 2002: 107 spindle whorls, many for very fine thread; light loom weights; 33 bone needles, perhaps for sailcloth; two antler ribbon-weaving combs, matched only at Birka

sites.name: The rivet bank
sites.see: The upstream end of the bank. A boat lies on her side on rollers with three strakes off, and a man drives old rivets out of them into a basket. Beyond him a fire of grey boat planks burns with a green edge where the iron was. New oak lies split, not sawn. It smells of tar, and of the river.
sites.source: Callmer 2002: over 2,400 boat rivets, ship repair 'a major activity', old boat timber burnt; the waterfront is the least-dug part

sites.name: Asbod's house
sites.see: A house on the ground like the others, ten paces long, with the door open and a bench outside it. Inside, a long hearth, a vat, smoke under the roof, and men of four peoples sitting where they can see the door. On a flat stone by the fire somebody is moving amber pieces across scratched squares. It smells of malt and wet wool. An ale-house, though nobody here has a word for it.
sites.source: invented; the house size and three amber gaming pieces from Callmer 2002; a guest's needs from Hávamál 2-4 (Bellows 1923)

sites.name: The old market ground
sites.see: Across the river and a little upstream: a stretch of grazing where the village of Yngsjö keeps its cattle. Nothing stands on it. Underfoot, wherever a hoof has cut the turf, the sand is full of glass: drops, rods and broken beads in blue, white and yellow. In the bank below it a pale cliff of clay shows where men have dug.
sites.source: Callmer 2002: Åhus I, about 700 to 750, over 70,000 pieces of glass waste, grazing land of Yngsjö after; kaolin dug from the bank for crucibles. That the dead are remembered on this ground is the game's choice: no grave field is reported (?)

sites.name: The still water
sites.see: A slow bend above the town where the brown water stands almost still under an alder. No building, no post, no fence. A flat stone at the edge is worn smooth, and there is a smear of fat on it. People lower their voices here without being told, and nobody waters cattle at this spot.
sites.source: INVENTED (?): no shrine has been found at Åhus. The river's name means the holy or luck-bringing river, and why is not known (Wikipedia (sv) 'Helge å'); offerings in water are known elsewhere among the Danes (Tissø: Design/content/lore/gods_cult.md). The district's holy place may have been Vä, inland, whose name means one.

sites.name: The river-mouth landing
sites.see: The river meets the bay over sand, with surf on the bar in an easterly. A few boats are drawn up above the weed line, nets on poles, a farm's cattle standing in the shallows. Upriver, where the town was, there is ploughland. A woman sells from a chest lid; a boy watches your boat as if he means to remember her.
sites.source: Callmer 2002: abandoned in the later 9th century and ploughed; the landing and its trade are the game's guess, because the game keeps the port open (?)

sites.name: The herring shore
sites.see: North of the mouth, in autumn: small boats run up on the sand before noon, silver to the gunwales, and gulls over them like smoke. Women gut on boards, and the tubs want more salt than anyone has. By the winter nights the beach is empty and smells of it still.
sites.source: goods_793.json (herring made in skane); trade_year_793.json (September to November); Design/content/economy/food.md 192, 237. The great Skåne herring markets are later, about 1200: this is a beach, not a fair.

sites.name: The stone house
sites.see: A house of grey stone laid in mortar, twenty paces long and ten wide, standing by the river mouth with no thatch near it. The door is above a man's reach, up a ladder. Lime dust still whitens the grass. Nobody here has built in stone before, and the farmers come to look at it on feast days.
sites.source: Wikipedia (sv) 'Åhus borg': about 20 by 10 m, mid 11th century, perhaps Scandinavia's oldest stone castle. Who held it is not known; the door and the ladder are the game's guess (?)

people.name: Toke
people.trait: A comb-maker who also casts brooches and cuts amber, because one craft does not feed a plot. Remembers every hand he has sold to, by the hand and not the face.
people.want: Shed red-deer antler by the boatload each spring, and one buyer who comes back, so he need not sail the coast every summer at his age.
people.fear: That his sons will not learn the casting, and that the foreign goods which ended his father's bead-making will one day end his combs.
people.voice: Talks while he works and does not look up. Says less than he means, and measures everything in combs.
people.looks: About forty, lean, fair hair long over the brow and cut short at the neck, a leather apron white with antler dust, a fine saw in his hand and a finished comb pushed through his belt.
knows: what combs, brooches and amber fetch at every market from the Slie to the Svear's lake, since he has sold at them
who on the plots is at home and who is away with the ships
that his father made beads on the south bank until the foreign ones came
which farmers bring the best antler, and when

ties.note: his brother's widow: two families on one plot, and her thread pays for his bronze in a bad year
they cast the same brooch; Alle's pins hold better and Toke knows it
last spring's antler is not paid for yet
Sote mends the boat Toke sails the coast in, for combs
they set up side by side on the Slie each summer and watch each other's prices
bought bronze scrap of him on a promise; Asulf has not forgotten
Holmfast buys his combs for the east and counts them twice
a bead woman on the eastern lake buys one of each of his amber pendants and breaks it to see how it was made

lines.greet: A Frisian. Your cloak gives you away. Sit where the dust does not blow. Combs are in the chest, brooches on the peg. Touch what you like.
lines.greet_again: I know that hand. You took two dozen and paid fair weight. Did they sell, or have you come to complain?
rumour: My father made beads across the river. Then ships brought beads by the sack. He learned combs at forty. I keep that in mind.
Three plots are shut since the summer began. They are not dead. They are at the Slie, selling. They come home when the herring does.
A man from the Svear's lake wants combs with a case. A comb in a case is two combs' work. I told him two combs' price.
lines.saying: A hundred years of combs, and the dogs have eaten most of the proof.
lines.friend: I have cut your mark on the back plate of these. Nobody asked me to. Sell them as yours.
lines.farewell: Bring antler in spring. Shed, not cut. The deer drop it for nothing and the farmers charge me for bending down.

people.source: invented; the crafts, the plot and the travelling season from Callmer 2002; the name from the Danish stones (commonest of all: Design/content/peoples/danish.md 7)

people.name: Thjodvi
people.trait: Spins the finest thread on the bank and weaves patterned ribbon on a comb of antler. Sets riddles to strangers to see what they are made of.
people.want: Dyes she cannot get here, madder and woad, and somebody to tell her how the women of the Svear's lake weave the same ribbon.
people.fear: A winter when the men come home with nothing, and her daughters sold into other households as spinners.
people.voice: Quick, amused, never stops her hands. Asks a question and then answers it herself if you are slow.
people.looks: About thirty-three, small and straight, brown hair knotted at the neck, a strap dress held by two oval bronze brooches with a string of mixed beads between them, a spindle always turning from her left hand.
knows: what a full set of fine dress costs, piece by piece, and who made each piece
the weaver's riddle of the thing with eight feet
which thread goes into sailcloth and which into a lord's shirt
what the women say, which is everything the men have not been told

ties.note: her dead husband's brother; they share the plot and argue over the hut
Asbod hears the news first and Thjodvi hears it second
her daughter's daughter's daughter, who has the comb after her
a woman on the Svear's lake weaves ribbon on the same kind of comb; they have never met and each has seen the other's work
he answered her riddle once, years ago, and set her a harder one she still has not solved
she had the eight-footed riddle from the skald of the king's hall, who paid for a ribbon with it

lines.greet: You are looking at the ribbon. Everyone does. Look with your eyes. Now: what has eight feet and four eyes, and carries its knees above its belly?
lines.greet_again: The Frisian who thinks before he answers. Sit. I have a new thread for you to fail to break.
rumour: A set of dress for a bride went east last moon. Cloth, ribbon, brooches, beads, a comb. Five plots made it. One man sold it.
The men say the casting is theirs because of the fire. We let them say it. Who do they think sews the bellows?
A Wend offered me wax for thread. I took it. Now the casters come to me for wax for their moulds, and I name the price.
lines.saying: A weaver knows another weaver, even one with eight feet.
lines.friend: Sleep at our hearth when you are here. The boat is damp, and I want the news before Asbod has it.
lines.farewell: Bring me red dye and I will tell you what your wife should have asked you for.

people.source: invented; the fine thread, the ribbon combs and the beads from Callmer 2002; the riddle is Gestumblindi's 14, 'given by a weaver at the landing' in riddles_793.json r-gest-14 (Vigfusson and Powell 1883); the name from the Danish stones (Gørlev 1)

people.name: Alle
people.trait: A caster in bronze and a little silver who trusts a scale and nothing else. The man who will cut your penny in two in front of you and think nothing of it.
people.want: Clean silver, whatever is stamped on it, and scrap bronze that has not been stretched with lead.
people.fear: Bad metal in his crucible, and a name for short weight, which would end him on this coast in a season.
people.voice: Exact and unhurried. Names a weight, waits, and lets you be the one to speak next.
people.looks: About forty-five, thick in the arms, a short grizzled beard singed on one side, a wool cap, a folding bronze scale in a little box at his belt and a knife worn thin from nicking silver.
knows: what silver is worth by weight against any good on the bank
how to nick, bend and cut silver, and what plated copper looks like under the knife
that silver with the Saracens' writing comes from the east, and is purer than most kings' coin
why his brooch pins hold: a sprung plate where others coil a spring

ties.note: the same brooch from two plots; they borrow each other's moulds and deny it
buys Sote's burnt rivets for the iron, by the basket
they have never met: Sigimar's pennies come through his hands and he weighs each as if it were a lie
Holmfast left a ring with him against a weight of silver; the ring is still here
Ketil, a Dane who keeps a house and a scale among the Ests; they use weights off the same mould
a Gute who learned the sprung pin on this plot and took it home
the farmer does not trust the scale and cannot say why; Alle has stopped explaining

lines.greet: Put it in the pan. Your king's face I do not know. His silver I will know in a moment.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian with the whole pennies. They weighed true last time. I said so on the bank. Put them in the pan.
rumour: A man paid me with silver from the east last moon, with writing like worm tracks. Purest I have melted. I kept one piece uncut.
Your Frankish pennies are heavier this year than last. Somebody has told your king what silver is for.
A ring came to me, silver over copper. I cut it through and nailed both halves to the fence. The man has not come back.
lines.saying: A stamp is one man's word. A scale is the same for everyone.
lines.friend: Here. A scale that folds, and weights I cast myself. Now nobody between here and the Svear can tell you what your own silver weighs.
lines.farewell: Half a penny over. I do not keep what is not mine. Hold out your hand.

people.source: invented; the casting, the silver and the changed brooch pin from Callmer 2002; weighing, nicking and cutting from the spine (silver_road) and Design/content/economy/silver_coin.md; coins at Åhus are reported elsewhere, not in the paper read (?)

people.name: Sote
people.trait: Mends boats on the bank and builds one a winter. Reads a hull the way a farmer reads a cow: where she has been, how she was treated, what she will do next.
people.want: Straight oak, which this open country does not grow, and a second pair of hands he does not have to feed all year.
people.fear: A boat of his opening a seam at sea with a known man aboard.
people.voice: Slow and flat. Speaks of boats as she and of their owners as he who has her.
people.looks: About twenty-eight, tall, big-handed, sandy hair tied back with a thong, tar to the elbows, a bag of rivets and roves at his hip and a clench hammer through his belt.
knows: what your boat needs before you ask, and what it will cost in days
which hulls on the bank are for sale and why
the bar, the river's set, and where the surf breaks in an easterly
who came in from where, by the weed on her strakes

ties.note: keeps Toke's coasting boat tight, paid in combs
sells him the iron out of burnt planks
has drunk at her house every evening for three years and said nothing useful
learned the trade two winters on Gotland and still lays a keel the Gutes' way
his father's brother, a Dane who builds boats among the Wends at Reric and taught him to respect a pegged hull
a cousin across the sound in the king's following; Sote takes his friends over the bar
mended a Wend boat for him once and was paid in wax and a good word along that coast
the wright at the Slie says he only mends; Sote says a man who has never mended does not know what he built
mended a Wend boat beside the Wends' well-digger one summer at Reric; neither would use the other's nails

lines.greet: She is Danish-built, or close to it. Four oars. Somebody has looked after her. Draw her up here and I will look at her garboards.
lines.greet_again: Your boat again. She floats higher than she did. You have been selling. Has the fourth strake wept since I caulked it?
rumour: A Wend boat came in pegged with wood, no iron in her. She was tight. I looked a long time and did not say so.
I burnt a boat last moon that was older than my father. Two baskets of rivets out of her. She kept on working.
With the wind in the east the bar breaks white. Wait a tide. I have pulled three men out who would not wait.
lines.saying: A boat is never finished. She is only launched.
lines.friend: I would build you a bigger one over a winter. Bring the oak yourself and I will take off a third.
lines.farewell: Keep tar on her. If she weeps, come back. If she sinks, do not say my name.

people.source: invented; the rivets, the repairs and the burnt timber from Callmer 2002; the open country with little woodland from the same; the name from the Danish stones (DR 209)

people.name: Asbod
people.trait: Brews for the traders who sleep in their boats and remembers what every one of them owes, drinks and lets slip.
people.want: Malt and honey before the winter brewing, and news an hour before anyone else has it.
people.fear: A killing at her hearth, which would shut her door: the peace of this place holds only as long as everyone agrees it does.
people.voice: Warm, loud, and never asks a question she does not already half know the answer to.
people.looks: About thirty-eight, broad and red-armed, fair hair under a linen cloth, a grey strap dress with one brooch not matching the other, a dipper hanging from her belt.
knows: who is on the bank, where from, and what he carries
which hands are looking for a ship and why they left the last one
that nobody takes a toll here by right, and who has tried
how to seat a Wend, a Svea and a Dane at one fire so that all three walk out

ties.note: news goes between them faster than a boat
she knows why he comes and is waiting to see whether he will ever say it
buys his barley for malt and pays in ale, which suits him too well
he brought a lot of captives to her door once and she shut it; he tells men her ale is thin
he sat on her bench before he went south; she kept his place a year
they send each other greetings by every skipper and have done for ten years without meeting
the Wend woman who turns her greetings to the ale-wife at Reric, and adds news of her own

lines.greet: A new face, and a boat with a tent on her. There is fire, water and a bench. Ale is silver, by Alle's weight. Sit by the door till I know you.
lines.greet_again: You. Further in this time. The man in your old seat is from Gotland and says he is from nowhere. What did you bring me to tell?
rumour: A great man inland sent to say the bank owes him a share. We sent back a comb. Nobody has come to argue.
Two of the amber pieces are gone from my board. I know who. He will put them back when he loses at something else.
Ships from the west talk of a church burnt on an island and silver going cheap. I have not seen any of it here. Yet.
lines.saying: The herd knows when to go home from the grass. Drinkers I have to tell.
lines.friend: Your cup hangs on that peg now. Nobody else drinks from it. If you want a hand for the boat, ask me first, not the bench.
lines.farewell: Go with the wind, and come back with something worth hearing.

people.source: invented; the role from npc_roles_793.json (alewife); her saying turns Hávamál 21 (texts_793.json havamal_021, Bellows 1923); market peace that 'protected only briefly' and the town's freedom from Callmer 2002

people.name: Hebbi
people.trait: A farmer of Yngsjö, a morning's walk up the river, who grazes the old market ground and sells the town its antler, amber, barley and beef. Knows old verses and gives them away cut on sticks.
people.want: A fair weight for what he carries in, and iron: a new share for his plough, a cauldron that does not leak.
people.fear: The town folk, a little: too many of them, too clever, and paying in silver he cannot test himself.
people.voice: Slow, sidelong, fond of a proverb. Answers a question with what his father said.
people.looks: About thirty-five, heavy-shouldered and weathered, a brown wool tunic to the knee, leg wrappings, a sack of antler on his back and a short stick cut with runes stuck in his belt.
knows: where shed antler lies in spring and where amber washes up after an easterly
old sayings and question-verses, and which sticks he has cut them on
who inland calls himself great, and how far his word really reaches
what the cattle turn up on the old market ground

ties.note: sells him antler every spring and is always owed for the last lot
her malt is his barley; he drinks his payment
does not trust the scale and cannot say why; Alle has stopped explaining
a cousin who herds on the king's isle and gives away the same two verses at that market
sends her honey from the woods by any boat going west, and is paid a year behind
says he gave a Northman a verse on a stick once and was set a question he is still chewing

lines.greet: You buy? Antler, shed this spring. Amber from the shore, a sackful. I want iron or a fair weight. I will know if it is not fair. Somehow.
lines.greet_again: The stranger who paid what he said. That is rare enough to remember. I kept the best tines back.
rumour: My cattle graze where the old market was. They come home with glass in their hooves. Blue, mostly.
After an easterly the amber lies on the sand like barley after threshing. You only have to be there before my neighbour.
Men inland go to the holy place at the turn of the year. I go. I do not say what is done. You were not asked.
lines.saying: The witless man lies awake all night thinking of everything. In the morning his trouble is where he left it.
lines.friend: Here. A stick. My father's verse about the two who hide in the wood when everything ends. Keep it dry.
lines.farewell: Go well. Do not water at the still bend. That is not for boats.

people.source: invented; Yngsjö's grazing and the antler and amber trade from Callmer 2002; he is the 'Skane farmer' and the 'farmer at the market' who gives texts_793.json t-vafth-45, havamal_021 and havamal_023 (Bellows 1923); the name is a Dane's in the Royal Frankish Annals 811

people.name: Tonna
people.trait: Born on a plot of the old town and carried out of it as a child. Sells cloth, combs and other people's amber from a chest lid at the river mouth, and keeps her great-grandmother's ribbon comb and her riddles.
people.want: The town back, which she will not get, or failing that a share in a ship that sails where the craftsmen went.
people.fear: That she is the last who can say whose plot was whose.
people.voice: Dry and exact, with a habit of naming the dead as if they had stepped out for a moment.
people.looks: About forty, spare, grey already in her brown hair, a blue strap dress with two old oval brooches worn smooth, a small antler comb with a row of slots hanging at her belt.
knows: where the town's families went: the Slie, the Svear's lake, a place nearer by
a question-verse about the sun's daughter, cut on a stick, for whoever comes asking the right way
what weighed silver buys now that the east is pouring it in
which ships on the Baltic road are worth hailing

ties.note: her mother's mother's mother; Tonna has her comb and half her riddles
an English skipper who put in for water and asked more questions than any buyer; she answered them
took walrus rope of him at the Slie on a promise of cloth; the cloth is woven and waiting
keeps the fourth stick of the Svea skald's chain of question-verses, given to her brother the pilot against a fare, and hands it on to whoever has earned the one before
a Gute house that buys her cloth and tells her nothing about its silver
a smith on the king's isle who has her antler for tool handles and is a season behind in paying
sent combs and amber east to him on trust, and a riddle with them; he has answered the riddle and not yet sent the furs
her brother Erik, the pilot of the river mouth, who was given the stick she keeps
a goldsmith at the Slie is of the families that left the town; his moulds were on the next plot to hers (?)

lines.greet: You are looking for a town. It was up there, where the barley is. I was born on the fourth plot from the bank. What do you want to buy?
lines.greet_again: The Frisian house. Your people bought combs of mine. Of my people's. Sit. The chest lid is the market now.
rumour: An Englishman sailed past for the Este's country and put in for water. He asked who we pay. I said: whoever comes.
The plough turned up a mould for a brooch last spring. My uncle's. I knew the pattern. The farmer gave it to his child to play with.
Silver from the east is so common now that men bury it and forget where. Not here. Here we never had enough to forget.
lines.saying: A town is plots and a reason. Take away the reason and you have good ploughland.
lines.friend: Thjodvi asked your forefather a riddle. He answered. So I will ask you one, and it is harder, and worth more.
lines.farewell: If you see our people at the Slie, tell them the river still runs.

people.source: invented; the abandonment and ploughing from Callmer 2002; she is the 'Skane trader' who holds r-vafth-46 of the chain 'dellings_door' from 871 (riddles_793.json); the name from a Skåne stone (Sövestad 2: peoples/danish.md 7)

people.name: Asgot
people.trait: The pilot of the river mouth, who was sixteen the summer the kings' fleets filled the bay and has told it every year since, a little differently. Signed with the cross, and keeps a hammer under his shirt for the bar.
people.want: To be believed, and a fee for every hull he takes over the sand.
people.fear: The stone house and whoever sits in it deciding that pilots are the lord's men too.
people.voice: Easy and long-winded, with a storyteller's pauses. Truthful about the water and less so about the battle.
people.looks: About forty, wiry, a cropped fair beard, a faded red wool cap, a short sea cloak pinned at the right shoulder, a sounding pole in his hand and a small silver cross on a thong.
knows: the bar and the river's set at every wind
what he saw of the fleets as a boy, and three other men's accounts of it that do not agree
who built the stone house, or at least who is living in it
what the king's penny weighs this year

ties.note: his father's people reckon themselves hers; he has the story of the town from them, fourth hand
held a bow line for one of the king's English ships, once, and has served the king in his own telling ever since
the priest who signed him with the cross, on the king's isle; Asgot sends him herring in Lent
a Gute who crosses the bar without a pilot and has been lucky nine times
the pilot of the bar four lifetimes back was of his kin; the marks are his, and so, they say, is the pole (?)
the bishop's man in the stone house asked whether he was baptised; he said 'signed', and has been preached at since

lines.greet: You will want taking in. The sand moved at the last full moon. A fee now, or a bigger one to Sote's grandson when you are aground.
lines.greet_again: I know your boat. She draws a hand more than you say she does. Follow my pole. Did I tell you about the fleets?
rumour: Some say the Northmen dammed the river and loosed it on the king's ships. I was here. I saw no dam. I saw a great deal of water.
Some say a bridge broke under the Danes. There is no bridge. There was never a bridge. Men lie better than they build.
The stone house has a door you reach by ladder. A man who wants to keep you out that badly means to take something from you.
lines.saying: Both kings won. Ask either side. Only the river lost men it had no use for.
lines.friend: I will tell you the truth about that summer, since you have paid me four times without arguing. I hid in the reeds. All day.
lines.farewell: Keep the alder on your left hand until the water goes green. Then you are over.

people.source: invented; what he denies is Snorri's dam and Saxo's bridge (Wikipedia (en, sv) 'Battle of Helgeå'); the fight from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1025 (Ingram 1823); whether it was at this river is disputed, and so he is made an unreliable witness; the name from a Danish stone (Rønninge)

people.name: Erik
people.trait: The pilot of the river mouth in the years after the town: born on a plot, carried out of it as a child with his sister, and now the one man who knows where the bar lay last moon.
people.want: A fee for every hull over the sand, and somebody to hand the sounding pole to.
people.fear: An easterly with a stranger's ship on the bar and his name called afterwards.
people.voice: Short and salt. Answers a question about the town with one about your draught.
people.looks: About thirty, wiry, a fair beard bleached almost white, a sealskin cap, bare legs brown to the thigh, a sounding pole taller than himself marked in hand-breadths.
knows: the bar and the river's set at every wind
which ships on the Baltic road put in for water, and whose they are
what a Svea skald looks like when he is seasick
where the old plots lie under the barley, by the feel of the ground

ties.note: his sister, who keeps the stick he was given, since she can tell who has earned it
carried the Svea king's skald home sick from the sea, and was given the fourth stick of his chain against the fare
the pilot of the bar four lifetimes on is of his kin and uses his marks (?)
took the English skipper's ship over the bar for water, and was asked the name of every headland in sight

lines.greet: What does she draw? No, what does she really draw? Follow my pole. Keep the alder on your left hand.
lines.greet_again: Your boat again. The sand has moved a ship's length since you were here. So have I. Follow the pole.
rumour: A skald of the Svea king was sick the whole way over the sea. He paid his fare with a stick of runes. My sister says it is worth more than silver. She would.
An Englishman put in for water and asked the name of every headland. I told him. He said them back to me, in order, like a man counting sheep.
There was a town up the river. I was born in it. Now I know it by where the barley grows thin.
lines.saying: The bar is where it was last. That is all anyone knows about it.
lines.farewell: Out on the ebb, the alder on your right hand now. If the water goes brown, you have gone wrong.

people.source: invented: the 'pilot at the river mouth in Skane' of uppsalir.arnfast's tie, who holds the fourth stick of the chain 'Delling's door' against a fare (riddles_793.json r-vafth-46, found with a Skane trader from 871); brother of ahus.tonna. Wulfstan sailed past with Skane on his left hand about 890 (texts_793.json wulfstan). A landing at the river mouth in these years is the game's guess (?). The name is Erik (DR 1)

people.name: Thancrad
people.trait: Bishop Egino's man in Skane, lodged in the stone house at the river mouth: earnest, cold, and carrying more letters than a priest of so small a place should.
people.want: The farms of the river baptised in more than name, and his bishop's plan carried through without his name on it.
people.fear: The Svear's king saying no; and what his own bishop will ask of him then.
people.voice: Careful Danish learned from a book and a Bremen clerk. Asks whether a man is baptised before he asks his name.
people.looks: About thirty-five, thin, cropped dark hair round a tonsure, a black cloak clasped at the throat, a leather satchel of letters he never puts down, chilblains.
knows: which farms on the river have a cross on the wall and a hammer under the shirt
what Bishop Egino writes to the bishop at Sigtuna, since he carries it
what is said of the great temple of the Svear, at third hand
who sits in the stone house, and what share of the landing he takes

ties.note: carries the letters between his bishop Egino and the bishop at Sigtuna; knows the plan against the temple at Uppsalir, and prays it is not tried
asked the pilot whether he was baptised and was told 'signed'; neither has let it rest

lines.greet: Are you baptised? Good. Then your name. Forgive the order. Here I have learned to ask the first thing first.
lines.greet_again: The merchant. You go east? I have a letter for Sigtuna. It is sealed. It will stay sealed. I say so to everyone who carries one.
rumour: The pilot here says he is signed with the cross. I told him that is a door, not a house. He said he knows about doors. He keeps a hammer for the bar.
My bishop has brought the people of the eastern isle to the font, and broken their idols. He thinks the Svear's great temple would burn as well. Their king thinks not.
A house of stone. They come on feast days to look at it. I should like them to come for another reason.
lines.saying: Signed is a door. Baptised is the house. Most here live on the step.
lines.farewell: Go with God. If you pass the Svear's lake, say nothing of letters.

people.source: invented: 'Bishop Egino's man in Skane' of uppsalir.adalvard's tie. Egino was bishop at Dalby from about 1060 and at Lund from 1066, and brought Bornholm and Blekinge to baptism; he and Adalvard the Younger planned to destroy the temple at Uppsalir, and King Stenkil refused (Adam of Bremen IV.8-9, IV.30, by way of the dossier of Uppsalir; not opened) (?). That he lodges in the stone house at the river mouth is the game's (?): who held it is not known. The name is Thancrad (names_placeholder.json, Saxon)

stories.title: The halved penny
stories.summary: At Dorestad a penny is a penny because the king says so. On the bank at Ahus a caster puts yours in a pan, finds it a little over, and cuts it in two with a chisel to make the weight: the first time a Frisian sees a coin cut in half on purpose.
stories.picture: A caster's blackened hands over a small bronze folding scale on a chest lid: in one pan lead weights, in the other half a silver penny, the other half lying beside the chisel; a Frisian in a short cloak staring at it.

beats.text: Sigimar the moneyer says that north of the Eider men cut the king's coin like cheese. He does not believe it of any people who can cast bronze. He would give something to see such a piece.

Alle weighs your pennies, nicks one with his knife to see the colour inside, and cuts another across the king's name to make the weight come even. He hands you the half you are owed. He does not understand why you are looking at him.

On the bench they are laughing, kindly, at the Frisian who counted his silver instead of weighing it. A Gute says that at home a man gets his penny's weight, not its name. Asbod says Alle sells scales.

Holmfast weighs your silver three times and finds that Alle's weights and his own agree to a grain. He has silver with the Saracens' writing, whole and in quarters. Yours, he says, is the first Frankish coin he has not had to test.
Sigimar turns the half penny and the cut dirham over for a long time. He weighs both. He says the Saracen's is better silver than the king's, and that you are not to repeat it.
At Ripa a goldsmith says the same thing in other words: silver has one face, and it is the inside. He sells the scale for three ounces.

endings.how: Bought a folding scale and weights from Alle and let him teach the nick and the bend.
endings.text: Nobody on this bank weighs your silver twice again. Ravn nods, once. Aldger says a king's penny was good enough for his father, and counts his own purse by tale all the same.
endings.reward: A folding scale and Alle's lead weights; Alle friendly; no short weight at Ahus, and the scale counts toward the spine's sv_scale at Paviken; a word on what silver buys along the coast.

endings.how: Refused to have pennies cut and paid by count, at whatever the count was called.
endings.text: You pay a tenth more than a man with a scale and are known for it from here to the Svear's lake as the Frisian who counts. It is said without malice. It is said for years.
endings.reward: Nothing but pride kept whole; a standing joke that opens benches to you in every Danish landing (a small gain in standing there, a small loss in the purse).

endings.how: Took the cut halves and a quartered dirham back to Sigimar at Dorestad.
endings.text: Sigimar keeps the pieces in a box with his trial weights and shows them to nobody. He takes your word on silver after that, which he takes from no one.
endings.reward: Sigimar's trust (the spine's sv_moneyer_trusts): foreign silver changed at Dorestad at the lesser loss; 60 d for the pieces; Alle's name known in the upper town.

stories.reward: The scale, or the moneyer's trust, or a name on the coast: the player comes away knowing that silver has two prices, a stamped one and a weighed one.

stories.title: The thing with eight feet
stories.summary: A weaver on the bank asks every stranger the same riddle and gives her hearth to whoever answers. Three generations on, when the town is barley, a woman with the same ribbon comb is holding one stick of a longer chain, and remembers whose house answered the first.
stories.picture: A sunken hut seen from its doorway: a small woman with a spindle turning from her left hand, looking up at the viewer with one eyebrow raised; in the corner of the door frame above her, a spider in its web against the light.

beats.text: Thjodvi asks what has eight feet and four eyes and carries its knees higher than its belly. She gives you three tries, and the women stop spinning to listen. Ravn, if he is aboard, looks at the roof and says nothing.
You have it: a weaver like herself. She hangs your cloak by her own fire. She says a man of the king's hall on the isles paid for a ribbon with that riddle, and that he has harder ones he sells dear.
The king's skald knows Thjodvi's ribbon when he sees it on your sleeve. He says a woman who pays in thread deserves better riddles than she got, and sets you one to carry back to her.
A weaver on the Svear's lake is working ribbon on a slotted antler comb, the twin of Thjodvi's. She wants to know who taught the other woman. So, it turns out, does Thjodvi.

Tonna sells from a chest lid where the river meets the bay. The comb at her belt is Thjodvi's. If you come with the answer to the stick before hers, she hands you a verse about the sun's daughter, and says your house was always quick.

endings.how: Answered the riddle within the tries (riddles_793.json r-gest-14).
endings.text: You sleep dry at Ahus from then on, and hear what the women know a day before the bench does. The welcome passes to your heir with the comb's.
endings.reward: Lodging at Thjodvi's hearth whenever you lie here (rw_lodging); Thjodvi friendly; the women's news; from 871, Tonna gives the sun's-daughter stick of Delling's door without a price.

endings.how: Brought the skald's harder riddle from Hleidr and the Birka weaver's question back to her.
endings.text: Thjodvi works at the skald's riddle all winter and has it by the first day of summer. She weaves you a ribbon with a pattern nobody else on the coast will have, and says who it is from.
endings.reward: A patterned ribbon worth 60 d, or far more as a gift in a hall; Thjodvi a fast friend; a tie made between her and the weaver at Birka, who sells you her own work at the maker's price.

endings.how: Used the three tries and did not find it.
endings.text: She tells you the answer and laughs, and sells you thread at the stranger's price. You may ask again next year: she will have a different one.
endings.reward: Nothing lost but face; the riddle's answer in your notes; another try, with another riddle, after a winter.

stories.reward: A hearth that knows you, across three generations, and a place on the chain of Delling's door.

stories.title: Calfskin with marks on it
stories.summary: In 829 the monk Anskar is robbed at sea of nearly forty books on his way to the Svear. Not long after, a dealer on the open place is laying his amber out on a square of pale skin covered in black marks, and has a heap more of it under a hide.
stories.picture: A hide thrown back from a heap of books with their boards torn off, pages swollen with damp; on top, one open leaf with a large painted letter, and three lumps of raw amber sitting on it as on a cloth.

beats.text: Word on the Slie: the Frankish monk who sailed for Birka came there on foot with nothing. Pirates took his ship, his gifts for the king, and a chest of books. Nobody can say what a pirate wants with books.
A dealer has the books without their boards. The gold and the stones went to a caster on the fire plots weeks ago. He asks 90 d for the heap, as skin, and wonders why you are counting the leaves.
On the fire plots a caster is cutting a gilt mount with a cross on it into two brooch backs. He will sell you the uncut half for its weight. He says the work is good and the pattern is unlucky.
The monks at Birka have one psalter between them, copied from memory. They take the wet heap leaf by leaf, laying each on the grass to dry, and one of them weeps over a page of plain accounts.
At the Slie the bishop's school has twelve boys and one psalter. He will take any book a merchant brings, as a gift or at a fair price, and asks where leaves are sold for scraping.

endings.how: Bought the heap and carried it to the monks (sets ch_mission_north_books_bought).
endings.text: The price comes back from the bishop's own hand, with more, and your name is read at the altar in a place where few names are. A heathen dealer learns what skin is worth and is grateful, in his way.
endings.reward: The 90 d back and a gift on top at the chain's next step; standing with the mission and its friends; the spine's bk_carried; the dealer friendly.

endings.how: Bought the heap and sold the one sound book in Francia (sets ch_mission_north_books_sold).
endings.text: A book without boards fetches a year's profit from an abbot who does not ask where it has been. The bishop hears of it years later, and so does every monk who writes letters.
endings.reward: One book, 360 d where books are wanted; monks who know of it are cool to you for a generation.

endings.how: Told the dealer who pays for such things and kept your silver (sets ch_mission_north_4_told).
endings.text: The dealer keeps the heap dry after that. Years later the bishop buys his own psalter back from a man at Ahus who knows exactly what to ask.
endings.reward: Nothing spent; the dealer a friend who puts odd things aside for you; a small word in your favour when the mission hears how the books were saved.

stories.reward: The step of the chain 'mission_north' that falls here; the player learns what a book is worth in a market that cannot read one.

stories.title: The year they burnt the fences
stories.summary: A town is plots and a reason. In the 840s and 850s the reason goes: the buyers are at the Slie and the Svear's lake, and each winter fewer hearths are lit on the bank. The family that knows you must choose where to go, and has no ship of its own.
stories.picture: A winter dusk on the bank: a row of empty plots with their wattle fences pulled down and burning in a heap, one sunken hut already roofless; in front, a family loading a chest, a loom and a dog into a small boat.

beats.text: The open place has grass in it. Four dealers sit where forty sat in your father's time. The brooches are still the best on the coast, of the new long pattern, and there is nobody to sell them to.

Toke's grandson is casting on his grandfather's plot. He asks what you would do: go to the Slie, where the king takes a share; to the Svear's lake, where they know his work; or to the new place down the coast, where his neighbours went. He asks whether you would carry them.

A caster from Skåne has a booth by the Slie and his grandfather's moulds. He pays the king's man without complaint and says the buyers come to him now. He has put your mark beside his own on the booth post.
Barley stands where the plots were. The plough turns up antler and green bronze, and a child is playing with half a clay mould. Somebody at the landing knows whose it was.
Two generations before the fences burn, the town's comb-makers already spend their summers in the pit-houses by the Slie, beside the men they will one day move in next to.
In the full years a stranger can lay down a stake on a craftsman's plot at the winter nights and have it back in spring as combs and brooches with his own mark on them.

endings.how: Carried the household and its moulds to Sliesthorp.
endings.text: They prosper under the king's peace and pay for it. You have a craftsman's house on the Slie that sells to you first and at the maker's price, for as long as his line lasts.
endings.reward: Brooches and combs at source prices at Sliesthorp; a lodging there; the family fast friends across generations.

endings.how: Carried them the long way to Birka.
endings.text: It is five days' sail and they are sick for three. On the Svear's lake the weaver with the twin comb takes them in. They send you a brooch each year by whatever ship is going, until the year no ship goes.
endings.reward: A friend's house at Birka and its word with the town's keeper; a yearly gift worth about 24 d; a harder road, and a warmer welcome.

endings.how: Lent them the price of a boat of their own and let them choose.
endings.text: They go a little way down the coast with their neighbours, and nobody writes down where. The loan comes back in combs over six years. Their daughter sells from a chest lid at the river mouth, and knows your house.
endings.reward: The loan repaid in goods (about 300 d of combs and brooches over six years); Tonna's goodwill from 865; the old town's families speak for you wherever they went.

stories.reward: A craftsman's house that owes you its new start, in one of three places on the chart.

stories.title: Both kings won
stories.summary: In the summer of 1025 or 1026 King Cnut comes to the Holy River with an English and Danish fleet, and the kings of the Svear and the Northmen meet him there. A merchant caught in the bay can sell to one fleet, to the other, or to neither, and afterwards every man he meets will tell him a different battle.
stories.picture: The river mouth seen from the dunes of the sand bar: the bay beyond it packed with striped sails and gilded prows from edge to edge, smoke rising behind; in front, one small trading boat pulled high into the reeds, and a boy holding her bow line.

beats.text: The king's ships are fitting out below the bridge. Ship-bread, ale, rope and salt meat are bought up as fast as they are landed, and the price is whatever is asked. They say he is going to Denmark. Nobody says why with a fleet.

beats.when: year >= 1025 and year <= 1026 and month >= 5 and month <= 9
beats.text: There are more ships in the bay than you have seen in your life, and they are not all one king's. A boy of sixteen takes your bow line and says you had better choose a side of the river and stay on it. Both sides want food.
Asgot the pilot tells you about the fleets. There was no dam, he says, and there was never a bridge. Then he tells it again with a dam in it, because that is the one people pay for.

At London they say the king won at the Holy River and now writes himself king of part of the Svear. A monk who keeps the annals has written that the Swedes held the field. He asks whether you were there.

endings.how: Sold your cargo to Cnut's stewards on the south side.
endings.text: They pay in good English pennies, by tale, and want more. A steward cuts your name on a stick. When the king holds the whole road from London to the Baltic, that stick is worth having.
endings.reward: Double price for food and ship's stores; the king's men at London and Hleidr friendly; Svear and Northmen who hear of it cool.

endings.how: Sold to the Svear and the Northmen on the north side.
endings.text: They pay by weight, in hack and rings, and less than the English would have. But they hold the field at evening, by one account, and a Svea skipper remembers who came to his side of the river.
endings.reward: A fair price in weighed silver; a friend among the Svear at Birka's successor markets; a mark against you with the king's reeves for a few years.

endings.how: Drew the boat into the reeds upriver and waited it out.
endings.text: You see a great deal of water and very little battle, like everyone else. Afterwards you take three wounded men off the sand for nothing, from whichever side they were. Asgot, who hid beside you, is your friend for life.
endings.reward: No profit; a good deed known on both shores; Asgot a fast friend, who pilots you free and tells you, alone, what he saw.

stories.reward: Profit, or a king's stick, or a pilot's friendship: and the knowledge that the annals and the skalds do not agree.

works.name: A plot on the bank
works.what: A fenced plot of your own on the river strip, with a hut sunk into the sand for a store. A stranger may hold one for as long as his neighbours agree he may.
works.picture: A square of wattle fence on sand above the river, a low thatched hut sunk to its eaves inside it, a chest and bundles of antler under the roof, and the player's boat drawn up below.
works.needs: Two craftsmen of the town to speak for you (Toke and one other at friendly or better).
works.gives: A dry store at Ahus for goods left over winter; lodging without fee; the plot-holders treat you as one of the bank, and you may winter here.
works.source: Callmer 2002: plots of about 25 by 20 m, sunken-floored huts as workshops and stores, guest craftsmen from other markets. That a foreign merchant held one is the game's guess (?)

works.name: A hauling way
works.what: A way of oak rollers and a turning post at the rivet bank, so that a laden hull can be drawn clear of the river by six men instead of twenty.
works.picture: Oak logs laid like a ladder up a sandy bank from the water, a stout post with a rope turned round it at the top, and six men hauling a clinker boat up stern first.
works.needs: Sote at friendly or better, and oak brought in: the country here grows little.
works.gives: Repairs and careening at Ahus take a third fewer days, for you and for everyone; Sote puts your boat first; the bank remembers who paid.
works.source: Callmer 2002: over 2,400 rivets, ship repair 'a major activity', little woodland. The rollers themselves are invented in the period's manner (?)

works.name: A stake in a workshop
works.what: Bronze, silver and antler laid down on a craftsman's plot in autumn, to be worked over the winter and shared in spring: goods put together, as partners do.
works.picture: A sunken workshop in winter lamplight: a craftsman bent over a bench of comb plates, and beside him a chest with the player's mark on it, half full of finished combs and paired brooches.
works.needs: A craftsman at friendly or better, and the goods laid down before the winter nights.
works.gives: Each spring, combs and brooches worth about twice the stake at their selling price elsewhere, marked as yours; the craftsman need not sail the coast that summer and is at home when you call.
works.source: Callmer 2002: craftsmen wintered at home and worked for the whole coast. The partnership is modelled on the later félag, not attested before the 11th-century stones (?)

works.name: A stone at the river mouth
works.what: A standing stone cut with runes and painted, raised by the landing for a dead man of the house, the crew or the partnership.
works.picture: A tall grey stone by a sandy track above the river mouth, a band of red-painted runes running up one edge and over the top, a small boat passing on the water behind.
works.needs: A death to remember, and a rune-carver brought from inland.
works.gives: The dead man is remembered (act:remember); standing with every Dane who reads it; your heirs are known at this landing by the stone.
works.source: The fashion from about 970; Skåne stones of these years in runes_793.json (Sjörup DR 279, 'he fled not at Uppsala'; Valleberga DR 337). No stone is known at Åhus itself; one stands at Älleköpinge near by, text not checked (?)

ships.how: bought second-hand on the bank, or built to order over a winter
ships.picture: A four-oared clinker boat on rollers on a sandy river bank, new strakes pale against old dark ones, a tar pot smoking beside her.
ships.note: The boat of every plot that sails the coast in summer: Sote always has one mended and for sale. Close kin to the house's own.
ships.source: Callmer 2002 (clinker boats, by the rivets); story/ships_793.json norse_small_boat (built at ahus, 250 d)

ships.how: bought second-hand and made good here; built to order only if you bring the oak
ships.picture: A long lean ship of a dozen oars lying on her side on the bank with three strakes off, a shipwright sighting along her keel.
ships.note: The wrights here repair more than they build, and the country is short of long oak: a tired ship from the Slie or the isles is bought cheap, stripped and re-riveted. Slower than a new one and half the price.
ships.source: Callmer 2002: repair 'a major activity', old boat timber burnt, little woodland. That whole ships changed hands here is the game's guess (?)

ships.how: bought second-hand from a Wend or an Este trader on the bank
ships.picture: A broad shallow boat pegged with wooden nails, drawn up beside the Danish boats and looking foreign among them, a Wend skipper sitting on her gunwale.
ships.note: Traders of the south shore lie on this bank and sometimes sell the boat with the cargo. Pegged with wood, not iron: Sote does not like her and cannot fault her.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json baltic_coastal_boat; traders of other peoples at the site, Callmer 2002. The sale is invented (?)

sayings.text: The herds know well when home they shall fare, and then from the grass they go; but the foolish man his belly's measure shall never know aright.
sayings.source: Hávamál 21, tr. H. A. Bellows (1923): texts_793.json havamal_021; given here on a stick by a farmer at the market

sayings.text: The witless man is awake all night, thinking of many things; care-worn he is when the morning comes, and his woe is just as it was.
sayings.source: Hávamál 23, tr. H. A. Bellows (1923): texts_793.json havamal_023

sayings.text: What was that wonder: it has eight feet, four eyes, carrying its knees higher than its belly?
sayings.source: Gestumblindi's riddle 14 (the spider), tr. G. Vigfusson and F. York Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale (1883): texts_793.json t-gest-14. Written down in the 13th century; said, the game supposes, long before.

sayings.text: A stamp is one man's word. A scale is the same for everyone.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the practice from Design/content/economy/silver_coin.md

sayings.text: A Frisian counts his silver. A Dane weighs it. A Svea weighs it, and then weighs the Dane.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, after the spine's tone notes (a Svea trader counts everything twice)

sayings.text: A hundred years of combs, and the dogs have eaten most of the proof.
sayings.source: invented; the fact is the dig's: a century of comb-making left waste for only 160 to 350 combs, the rest rotted or gnawed (Callmer 2002)

sayings.text: Both kings won. Ask either side.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the Chronicle gives the field to the Swedes, the skald Ottar the Black praises Cnut for the victory (Wikipedia (sv) 'Slaget vid Helgeå')

sayings.text: A boat is never finished. She is only launched.

easter_eggs.text: By Asbod's hearth lies a slab of sandstone with round hollows ground into it, each the size of a thumb's end. Men shape gaming pieces in them. Three pieces on her board are amber.
easter_eggs.source: Callmer 2002: a sandstone slab with cup-shaped hollows, perhaps for shaping gaming pieces; three amber gaming pieces

easter_eggs.text: Look closely at a brooch from Alle's plot and one from Toke's: on Toke's the pin turns on a coiled spring, on Alle's on a flat sprung plate. Nobody can say why the town changed from one to the other.
easter_eggs.source: Callmer 2002: the pin changed here from a coiled spring to a sprung plate, for no reason anyone can see

easter_eggs.text: The little axe-shaped pendants of amber on Toke's bench are not hammers, and he will not say what they are for. He says they sell.
easter_eggs.source: Callmer 2002: amber beads and small axe-shaped pendants; their meaning is not given

easter_eggs.text: On the old market ground the turf is full of glass. Toke's father's work lies there with the rest: more than seventy thousand drops, rods and spoiled beads.
easter_eggs.source: Callmer 2002: over 70,000 pieces of glass waste at Åhus I

easter_eggs.text: Thjodvi's ribbon comb has a twin, and only one: on the Svear's lake.
easter_eggs.source: Callmer 2002: two antler ribbon-weaving combs, matched only at Birka

easter_eggs.text: The casters' crucibles are made of a white clay dug from the river bank under the old market. A crucible from here can be told from any other on the coast.
easter_eggs.source: Callmer 2002: kaolin dug from the bank for crucibles

easter_eggs.text: On the smith's scrap heap, among the cauldron sheet, is a hand's breadth of mail. He says it came in as scrap. There are very few weapons in this town.
easter_eggs.source: Callmer 2002: a piece of mail, few weapons

easter_eggs.text: Men of later days will write this place's name as Aos. It means the river's mouth, nothing more.
easter_eggs.source: Wikipedia (sv) 'Åhus': Aos, 1286 or 1296; the game's 'Áhús' is a back-formation

easter_eggs.text: From 871 a stick here asks: whence comes the sun to the smooth sky back, when Fenrir has snatched it forth? It is the fourth of five, and the fifth is at Uppsalir.
easter_eggs.source: Vafþrúðnismál 46, tr. H. A. Bellows (1923): riddles_793.json r-vafth-46, chain 'dellings_door'

unlocks.what: A hearth at Ahus: lodging at Thjodvi's fire
unlocks.gives: rw_lodging at Ahus; the women's news a day early (rumours here are a day fresher); passes to the heir, and from 865 to Tonna's chest lid.

unlocks.how: End 'The halved penny' by learning the scale, or reach friendly with Alle and pay 36 d.
unlocks.gives: No short weight at Ahus; counts toward the spine's flag sv_scale; act:weigh_silver and act:test_silver may be done aboard.

unlocks.how: Buy from Toke on three calls, or bring him shed antler twice.
unlocks.gives: Combs and brooches at the maker's price here (act:buy_at_source); goods marked as yours sell a little better where Toke's work is known; npc feeling carried to his heir.

unlocks.how: Commission it on the fire plots: 60 d and ten days.
unlocks.gives: A fitting for the boat (act:fit_upgrade): silver and small goods in the chest are not lost to a thief card in harbour.

unlocks.what: A sail mended and greased by the spinning huts
unlocks.how: Thjodvi at friendly or better; 30 d and five days.
unlocks.gives: A fitting for the boat (act:fit_upgrade): the sail's wear is made good and it holds a little closer to the wind until it wears again.

unlocks.what: Leave to winter on the bank
unlocks.gives: A winter at Ahus when the town is fullest: every craftsman is at home, and the winter's cards are drawn from this port.

unlocks.what: The sun's-daughter stick of Delling's door
unlocks.how: From 871, come to Tonna with the answer to the stick before hers (r-gest-15).
unlocks.gives: give_text t-vafth-46 and its riddle r-vafth-46; the last step of the chain is at Uppsalir (reward rw_hoard_spillings).

unlocks.what: Asgot takes you over the bar for nothing
unlocks.how: End 'Both kings won' in the reeds, or pay his fee four times without haggling.
unlocks.gives: act:hire_pilot at Ahus is free from 1030 to 1062; he tells you what he really saw.
